If it isn't and I want it, tell me how to enable it myself (Pro, Enterprise, or Education, not Home); don't change Windows features or reboot. Report native C++ toolchain requirements separately if I request AOT. L39: 4. Print a short summary of what was installed vs already present, then tell me to start a new Copilot CLI, activate the "winui-dev" agent, and to ask it to build an app. L40: ``` L41:

Clone the repo that maintains the plugin, then link its skills folder (the one containing `/SKILL.md` directories) into OpenCode's global skills directory, or a project's `.opencode/skills/`: L80: ```powershell L81: git clone L82: $src = "" L83: $dst = "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\opencode\skills" L84: New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $dst | Out-Null L85: Get-ChildItem $src -Directory | ForEach-Object { L86: $link = Join-Path $dst $_.Name L87: if (-not (Test-Path $link)) { New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path $link -Target $_.FullName | Out-Null } L88: } L89: ``` L90: The links are junctions, so `git pull` in the clone picks up skill updates. L91: ### Next steps L92: L93: Start a new session and ask for a real task, for example: L94: L95: > "Build me a WinUI 3 markdown editor with live preview and a custom title bar" L96: ## Updates L97: L98: When a catalog entry moves to a new version, update with your host's usual commands: L99: L100: ```powershell L101: copilot plugin marketplace update win-dev-skills; copilot plugin update @win-dev-skills L102: claude plugin marketplace update win-dev-skills; claude plugin update @win-dev-skills L103: codex plugin marketplace upgrade win-dev-skills L104: ``` -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/skills/main/skills/.curated/winui-app/SKILL.md) citeturn16view1 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/plain; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/skills/main/skills/.curated/winui-app/SKILL.md","lineno":null}); Total lines: 83 L0: --- L1: name: winui-app L2: description: Bootstrap, develop, and design modern WinUI 3 desktop applications with C# and the Windows App SDK using official Microsoft guidance, WinUI Gallery patterns, Windows App SDK samples, and CommunityToolkit components. L3: Use when creating a brand new app, preparing a machine for WinUI, reviewing, refactoring, planning, troubleshooting, environment-checking, or setting up WinUI 3 XAML, controls, navigation, windowing, theming, accessibility, responsiveness, performance, deployment, or related Windows app design and development work. L4: --- L5: # WinUI App L6: L7: Use this skill for WinUI 3 and Windows App SDK work that needs grounded setup guidance, app bootstrap, modern Windows UX decisions, or concrete implementation patterns. L8: ## Required Flow L9: 1. Classify the task as environment/setup, new-app bootstrap, design, implementation, review, or troubleshooting. L10: 2. If the task is about preparing a machine for WinUI, auditing readiness, or creating a brand new app, start with the bundled setup-and-scaffold flow in this skill before broader design, implementation, or troubleshooting work: L11: - Pick the app name when the request is for a new app. L12: - Use the exact name the user gave when it is already a safe folder name. L13: - If the user did not give a name, derive a short PascalCase name from the request and state what you chose. L14: - Create the project in the user's current workspace unless they asked for another location. L15: - Do not use `--force` unless the user explicitly asked to overwrite existing files. L16: - Run the bundled WinGet configuration from the skill directory so the relative path stays exactly `config.yaml`: L17: ```powershell L18: winget configure -f config.yaml --accept-configuration-agreements --disable-interactivity L19: ``` L20: - Treat the configuration as intended to enable Developer Mode, install or update Visual Studio Community 2026, and install the Managed Desktop, Universal, and Windows App SDK C# components needed for WinUI development. L21: - Assess the configuration result before continuing. Continue on success. If it fails, inspect the output instead of guessing. If the `winui` template is already available and the toolchain is usable, note the partial failure and continue. If prerequisites are still missing, stop and report the blocker clearly. L22: - Verify the template is available before scaffolding: L23: ```powershell L24: dotnet new list winui L25: ``` L26: - For diagnostics-only environment requests, explain that the bundled bootstrap may change the machine and get confirmation before running it. If the user declines changes, use the manual verification guidance in `references/foundation-environment-audit-and-remediation.md` and summarize readiness under `present`, `missing`, `uncertain`, and `recommended optional tools`. L27: - For a brand new app, scaffold with `dotnet new winui -o `. Add template options only when the user asked for them. Supported options: `-f|--framework net10.0|net9.0|net8.0`, `-slnx|--use-slnx`, `-cpm|--central-pkg-mgmt`, `-mvvm|--use-mvvm`, `-imt|--include-mvvm-toolkit`, `-un|--unpackaged`, `-nsf|--no-solution-file`, `--force`. Do not invent unsupported flags. If the user asks for packaged behavior, pass `--unpackaged false`. Otherwise keep the template default. L28: - Verify a new scaffold by confirming the expected project file exists and running `dotnet build` against the generated `.csproj`. L29: - Launch a newly scaffolded app through the correct path for its actual packaging model and confirm there is a real top-level window instead of relying only on the launcher process exit code. L30: 3. Read `references/_sections.md`, then load only the reference files that match the task. L31: 4. Make the packaging model explicit before creating or refactoring the app. Default to packaged for Store-like product workflows and Visual Studio deploy/F5 flows. Default to unpackaged when the user expects repeatable CLI build-and-run loops or direct `.exe` launches after each change. L32: 5. When the task is an opaque XAML compiler failure such as `MSB3073` or `XamlCompiler.exe`, read `references/foundation-template-first-recovery.md` and simplify back toward the current `dotnet new winui` scaffold for the chosen packaging model before inventing custom recovery structure. L33: 6. For any work that creates or changes a WinUI app, make a complete but minimal edit set, then build the app and run it before responding to the user. Do this by default even when the user did not explicitly ask for verification. If a running app instance locks the output while more work remains, stop it, rebuild, relaunch, and continue verification. L34: When the work is complete and launch verification succeeds, leave the final verified app instance running for the user unless they explicitly asked you not to. L35: 7. Treat launch verification as incomplete until the app shows objective success signals such as a responsive top-level window, expected window title, or other clear startup behavior. A spawned process by itself is not enough. L36: 8. Prefer Microsoft Learn for requirements, API expectations, and platform guidance. L37: 9. Prefer WinUI Gallery for concrete control usage, shell composition, and design details. L38: 10. Prefer WindowsAppSDK-Samples for scenario-level APIs such as windowing, lifecycle, notifications, deployment, and custom controls. L39: 11. Build toward WinUI and Fluent guidance first. Treat native WinUI shells, controls, interactions, and control chrome as the default implementation path. L40: 12. For grouped command surfaces such as document actions, editor formatting, view toggles, or page-level toolbars, favor a native `CommandBar` or other stock WinUI command surface before building a custom row with `Grid`, `StackPanel`, `Border`, or ad hoc button groupings. L41: 13. Do not invent app-specific controls, bespoke component libraries, or custom chrome to replace stock WinUI behavior unless the user explicitly asks for that customization, the existing product design system already requires it, or a verified platform gap leaves no clean native option. L42: 14. When customization is needed, first compose, template, or restyle built-in WinUI controls and system resources before adding CommunityToolkit dependencies or authoring a new custom control. L43: 15. Use CommunityToolkit only when built-in WinUI controls or helpers do not cover the need cleanly. L44: 16. Support both light and dark mode by default. Treat single-theme output as an exception that requires an explicit user request or an existing product constraint. L45: 17. Use theme-aware resources, system brushes, and WinUI styling hooks instead of hard-coded light-only or dark-only colors when building or revising UI. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Windows | Avalonia Docs (https://docs.avaloniaui.net/docs/platform-specific-guides/windows) citeturn16view2 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.avaloniaui.net/docs/platform-specific-guides/windows","lineno":null}); Total lines: 437 L0: 【0†iframe†www.googletagmanager.com】 L1: L2: 【1†Skip to main content】 L3: L4: * 【2†Welcome】 L5: * 【3†Supported platforms】 L6: * 【4†Getting Started】 L7: L8: * 【5†Fundamentals】 L9: L10: * 【6†XAML Reference】 L11: L12: * 【7†Layout】 L13: L14: * 【8†Styling】 L15: L16: * 【9†Data Binding】 L17: L18: * 【10†Data Templates】 L19: L20: * 【11†Property System】 L21: L22: * 【12†Events】 L23: L24: * 【13†Input & Interaction】 L25: L26: * 【14†Graphics and Animation】 L27: L28: * 【15†Custom controls】 L29: L30: * 【16†Services】 L31: L32: * 【17†App Development】 L33: L34: * 【18†Platform Integration】 L35: * 【18†Windows】 L36: * 【19†macOS】 L37: * 【20†Desktop Linux】 L38: * 【21†Embedded Linux】 L39: L40: * 【22†Android】 L41: L42: * 【23†iOS】 L43: * 【24†WebAssembly】 L44: * 【25†Platform-specific .NET】 L45: * 【26†Platform-specific XAML】 L46: * 【27†Testing】 L47: L48: * 【28†Deployment】 L49: L50: * 【29†Migration】 L51: L52: * 【30†How-To Guides】 L53: L54: * 【31†Samples & Tutorials】 L55: L56: * 【32†Breaking changes】 L57: * 【33†Troubleshooting】 L58: * 【34†Community Translations】 L59: * 【35†Enhanced Support†avaloniaui.net】 L60: * 【36†Professional Services†avaloniaui.net】 L61: * 【37†GitHub Discussions†github.com】 L62: * 【38†Blog†avaloniaui.net】 L63: L64: [Button: On this page] L65: # Windows L66: ## How Avalonia runs on Windows【39†​】 L67: L68: Avalonia uses the Win32 API directly on Windows. No additional workloads or dependencies are needed beyond the .NET SDK. Your target framework is simply `net9.0` or `net10.0`, not a platform-specific one. L69: Rendering uses Skia on top of Direct3D 11, reached through the ANGLE translation layer (the default `AngleEgl` mode described in 【40†Configuring Win32 platform options】), with an automatic software fallback when GPU acceleration is unavailable (for example, in remote desktop sessions or virtual machines without GPU passthrough). Input, windowing, clipboard, file dialogs, drag-and-drop, and accessibility are all provided through standard Win32 APIs. L70: Because there is no dependency on a Windows-specific .NET workload, you can cross-compile Windows builds from macOS or Linux. The resulting binary runs on any supported version of Windows with the .NET runtime installed. L71: ## Configuring Win32 platform options【40†​】 L72: `Win32PlatformOptions` controls how Avalonia renders, composites, and scales on Windows. Apply it by passing to `.With()` in the `AppBuilder` in `Program.cs`: L73: L74: `AppBuilder.Configure() L75: .UsePlatformDetect() L76: .With(new Win32PlatformOptions L77: { L78: RenderingMode = new[] L79: { L80: Win32RenderingMode.AngleEgl, L81: Win32RenderingMode.Software L82: }, L83: CompositionMode = new[] L84: { L85: Win32CompositionMode.WinUIComposition, L86: Win32CompositionMode.RedirectionSurface L87: }, L88: DpiAwareness = Win32DpiAwareness.PerMonitorDpiAware L89: }); L90: ` L91: The following options are available. L92: L93: * 【41†Rendering mode】 L94: * 【42†Composition mode】 L95: * 【43†DPI awareness】 L96: * 【44†Other options】 L97: ### Rendering mode【41†​】 L98: L99: `RenderingMode` is an ordered list of graphics backends. Avalonia tries each one in turn and uses the first that initializes successfully, so the first entry has the highest priority. The default is a two-item list of `AngleEgl` first, `Software` second. L100: Mode | Description L101: --- | --- L102: `AngleEgl` | GPU rendering through ANGLE EGL. Default GPU backend. L103: `Wgl` | GPU rendering through native Windows OpenGL. L104: `Vulkan` | GPU rendering through native Windows Vulkan. L105: `Software` | CPU rendering into a framebuffer. L106: ANGLE (Almost Native Graphics Layer Engine) translates the OpenGL ES calls that Skia produces into Direct3D 11 on Windows. This is why `AngleEgl` is the default GPU backend, and why it is the mode that 【42†`WinUIComposition` and `DirectComposition`】 depend on. L107: To support the widest range of devices, including remote desktop sessions and virtual machines without a GPU, include `Software` as a fallback. `RenderingMode` must contain at least one mode. If it is empty, or none of the listed modes initialize, Avalonia throws an `InvalidOperationException`. L108: ### Composition mode【42†​】 L109: L110: `CompositionMode` is an ordered list of window composition backends, tried in priority order like 【41†`RenderingMode`】. The default is a three-item list of `WinUIComposition` first, `DirectComposition` second, `RedirectionSurface` third. L111: Mode | Requirements | Behavior L112: --- | --- | --- L113: `WinUIComposition` | Windows 10 build 17134 and above. 【41†`RenderingMode`】 must include `AngleEgl`. | Supports acrylic effects and high refresh rate rendering. L114: `DirectComposition` | Windows 8 and above. 【41†`RenderingMode`】 must include `AngleEgl`. | L115: `LowLatencyDxgiSwapChain` | Feature Level 11_3, Windows 8.1 and above. 【41†`RenderingMode`】 must include `AngleEgl`. | Renders through a low-latency DXGI swap chain for reduced input latency, without the transparency and blur of `WinUIComposition`. L116: `RedirectionSurface` | | Compatibility fallback for older systems. Some Avalonia features may not work. L117: To support the widest range of devices, include `RedirectionSurface` as a fallback. If none of the listed modes apply, Avalonia throws an `InvalidOperationException`. L118: L119: For more information on how rendering and composition fit together, see 【45†Application architecture】. L120: ### DPI awareness【43†​】 L121: L122: `DpiAwareness` sets how the application responds to display scaling. The default is `PerMonitorDpiAware`. L123: L124: Value | Behavior L125: --- | --- L126: `PerMonitorDpiAware` | Adjusts the scale factor whenever DPI changes, such as when a window moves between monitors. L127: `SystemDpiAware` | Queries DPI once at startup and does not adjust to later changes. L128: `Unaware` | The application is DPI-unaware. The system bitmap-scales. L129: See 【46†High DPI and per-monitor scaling】 for more information on how scaling affects layout and assets. L130: ### Other options【44†​】 L131: Option | Type | Default | Description L132: --- | --- | --- | --- L133: `OverlayPopups` | `bool` | `false` | Embeds popups inside the window instead of creating separate top-level popup windows. L134: `WinUICompositionBackdropCornerRadius` | `float?` | `null` | When `CompositionMode` is `WinUIComposition`, creates rounded-corner blur brushes. Leave `null` for sharp corners. Use it for a rounded, blurred Windows 10 app or a borderless Windows 11 app. L135: `ShouldRenderOnUIThread` | `bool` | `false` | Renders on the UI thread instead of a dedicated render thread. Applies only when `CompositionMode` is `RedirectionSurface`. Intended for interop with systems that must render on the UI thread, such as WPF. L136: `WglProfiles` | `IList` | `4.0`, `3.2` | OpenGL profiles used when `RenderingMode` is `Wgl`. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Download & Installation | Kopia (https://kopia.io/docs/installation/) citeturn16view3 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://kopia.io/docs/installation/","lineno":null}); Total lines: 313 L0: # Download & Installation L1: ## Two Variants of Kopia L2: L3: Kopia is a standalone binary and can be used through a command-line interface (CLI) or a graphical user interface (GUI). L4: L5: * If you want to use Kopia via CLI, you will install the `kopia` binary; when you want to use Kopia, you will call the `kopia` binary (along with 【0†Kopia commands】) in a terminal/command prompt window or within a script. L6: * If you want to use Kopia via GUI, you will install `KopiaUI`, the name of the Kopia GUI. The installer for KopiaUI comes with the `kopia` binary and a graphical user interface called `KopiaUI` - a wrapper for the `kopia` binary. `KopiaUI` runs the `kopia` binary and associated commands as necessary, so you do not need to use the command-line interface. L7: > NOTE: `KopiaUI` is available both as a web-based application and a desktop application. The web-based application is available when you run Kopia in 【1†server mode】. For users who will be using Kopia to backup their individual machines and not running Kopia in server mode, you will use the desktop application. If you do not understand Kopia server mode, do not worry; download `KopiaUI` from the 【2†links below】, and you will get the desktop application by default. L8: Both the CLI and GUI versions of Kopia use the same `kopia` binary, so you are getting the same features regardless of which variant you decide to go with (since the `kopia` binary is the workhorse). However, some advanced features are available through CLI but have not yet been added to `KopiaUI`. L9: Right now, `KopiaUI` allows you to access all the essential features of Kopia that are required to backup/restore data: create and connect to repositories (including encryption), set policies (including compression, scheduling automatic snapshots, and snapshot retention), create snapshots, restore snapshots, automatically run maintenance, and install Kopia updates. L10: If you use `KopiaUI` and you want access to advanced features that are not yet available in `KopiaUI`, you can easily run the commands for those features via CLI by calling the `kopia` binary that comes with `KopiaUI`. In other words, using Kopia GUI does not restrict you from using Kopia CLI as well. L11: Kopia CLI is recommended only if you are comfortable with command-line interfaces (e.g., power users, system administrators, etc.). If you are uncomfortable with the command-line, use Kopia GUI. Although more limited than Kopia CLI, Kopia GUI is still very powerful and allows you to use Kopia to back up/restore your data easily. L12: ## Kopia Download Links L13: L14: The following installation options are available for the latest stable version of Kopia: L15: * 【3†Official Releases†github.com】 L16: * 【4†Windows CLI (Scoop)】 L17: * 【5†Windows GUI (`KopiaUI`)】 L18: * 【6†macOS CLI Homebrew】 L19: * 【7†macOS GUI Homebrew】 L20: * 【8†macOS GUI (`KopiaUI`)】 L21: * 【9†Debian/Ubuntu Linux (APT Repository, both CLI and `KopiaUI`)】 L22: * 【10†RedHat/CentOS/Fedora Linux (Linux YUM Repository, both CLI and `KopiaUI`)】 L23: * 【11†Arch Linux/Manjaro (AUR)】 L24: * 【12†OpenBSD】 L25: * 【13†FreeBSD】 L26: * 【14†Docker Images】 L27: The following options are available if you like to test the beta and unreleased versions of Kopia: L28: L29: * 【15†Test Builds†github.com】 on GitHub L30: * 【4†Windows CLI (Scoop)】 offers `test-builds` bucket L31: * 【6†macOS CLI Homebrew】 offers `test-builds` TAP L32: * 【9†Debian/Ubuntu Linux (APT Repository)】 offers `unstable` channel L33: * 【10†RedHat/CentOS/Fedora Linux (Linux YUM Repository)】 offers `unstable` channel L34: * 【16†Source Code†github.com】 - see 【17†compilation instructions】 L35: ## Installing Kopia L36: L37: CLI and GUI packages are available for: L38: L39: * Windows 10 or later, 64-bit (CLI binary, GUI installer {`KopiaUI`}, and Scoop package) L40: * macOS 10.11 or later, 64-bit (CLI binary, GUI installer {`KopiaUI`}, and Homebrew package) L41: * Linux - `amd64`, `armhf` or `arm64` (CLI binary and `KopiaUI` available via RPM and DEB repositories) L42: ### Windows CLI installation L43: L44: On Windows, Kopia CLI is available as a 【18†Scoop†scoop.sh】 package, which automates installation and upgrades. L45: L46: Using Scoop, installing Kopia is as easy as: L47: L48: `> scoop bucket add kopia https://github.com/kopia/scoop-bucket.git L49: > scoop install kopia L50: ` L51: L52: See the 【18†Scoop Website†scoop.sh】 for more information. L53: Alternatively, to install the latest unreleased version of Kopia use the following bucket instead: L54: L55: `> scoop bucket add kopia https://github.com/kopia/scoop-test-builds.git L56: ` L57: L58: You can also install Kopia CLI with `winget`. `winget` comes preinstalled with Windows 11 (21H2 and later), and is also available on Windows 10 via 【19†the Microsoft Store†apps.microsoft.com】. L59: L60: `> winget install Kopia.KopiaCLI L61: ` L62: ### Windows GUI installation L63: L64: The installer of `KopiaUI` is available on the 【3†releases page†github.com】.
